title: The Job Interview
paragraph: Tomorrow morning, I have an interview for a job I really want. I have ironed my shirt, printed two copies of my resume, and practiced my answers in front of the mirror. The hardest question will probably be, tell us about yourself, so I have prepared a short, honest answer. I plan to speak slowly and keep eye contact, even if my hands feel a little shaky. If I forget a word, I will pause, take a breath, and continue. Whatever happens, I know that preparing carefully is already a small victory.
tongue_twisters: Prepare, practice, and present with pride.
Careful candidates carry clean, crisp resumes.
Steady speakers speak with simple sincerity.

title: Cooking for the First Time
paragraph: When I moved into my own apartment, I could barely boil an egg. My first attempt at making curry filled the kitchen with smoke, and the neighbors knocked to ask if everything was alright. Slowly, though, I learned to measure spices, control the heat, and taste as I cooked. Now I enjoy chopping vegetables and listening to music while the onions turn golden. Cooking has taught me that patience matters more than talent, and that most mistakes are simply lessons with a pleasant smell.
tongue_twisters: Golden onions glisten in the great gray pan.
Fresh spices fill the kitchen with flavor.
Chop, stir, taste, and season slowly.

title: The Train Journey
paragraph: The train to the northern hills departs early in the morning, and I always choose a seat by the window. Outside, rice fields roll past, wide and green, with farmers bending low under the rising sun. A vendor walks down the aisle selling hot tea in small paper cups, and the smell of cardamom drifts through the carriage. I watch the villages appear and disappear, each one with its own tiny station and a handful of waving children. Long journeys give you time to think, and I find that thoughts are clearer when the world is moving.
tongue_twisters: Rolling rice fields run beside the railway.
Warm tea warms weary travelers.
Villages vanish behind the vibrating window.

title: Starting a Morning Walk Habit
paragraph: Three weeks ago, I decided to walk for twenty minutes every morning before work. The first few days were difficult because I wanted to stay in bed, but I forced myself to put on my shoes and step outside. Gradually, the streets became familiar, and I started to recognize the same faces: a man with a newspaper, a woman feeding pigeons, a boy walking his grandfather's dog. Now the walk is my favorite part of the day. It clears my mind, wakes up my body, and reminds me that small, steady habits can quietly change a life.
tongue_twisters: Morning walkers wander without worry.
Steady steps build strong, simple habits.
Pigeons peck and parade along the path.

title: A Rooftop Thunderstorm
paragraph: Yesterday afternoon, the sky turned dark gray within minutes. A cool wind swept across the rooftop, flipping the clothes on the line and sending leaves spinning through the air. Then the thunder rolled in, deep and slow, followed by a heavy curtain of rain. I stood under the stairway roof and watched the streets turn into small rivers. Children shouted happily and splashed through puddles, ignoring their mothers' calls. When the storm finally passed, the air smelled fresh and clean, and a pale rainbow stretched above the buildings.
tongue_twisters: Thunder rolls through the rainy, restless sky.
Children splash through shallow, silver puddles.
A pale rainbow rises after the rain.

title: Joining a Language Club
paragraph: Last month, I joined an English speaking club at my local community center. At first, I was nervous and spoke only when someone asked me a direct question. The members, however, were friendly and patient, and they never laughed at my mistakes. Each week, we choose a topic, share our opinions, and practice new vocabulary. I have noticed that my pronunciation is improving and that I feel more confident when I speak. Learning a language is not about being perfect; it is about showing up regularly and trying again.
tongue_twisters: Speak simply, speak slowly, speak clearly.
Friendly members practice pronunciation patiently.
Learning languages takes lots of little lessons.

title: The Old Bookshop
paragraph: At the end of my street, there is a tiny bookshop that smells of dust, paper, and old stories. The owner, Mr. Haque, sits behind a wooden desk with a pair of round glasses and a cup of tea. He knows the location of every book and can recommend something for every mood. Last week, he handed me a worn novel and said, this one will keep you company. He was right. I read it in three evenings, and now I visit the shop every Saturday, even when I do not plan to buy anything.
tongue_twisters: Dusty books and wooden shelves.
Mr. Haque hands me happy, handy hints.
Worn novels whisper wonderful stories.

title: Planning a Surprise Party
paragraph: My friends and I are planning a surprise birthday party for our classmate Nadia. We have booked a small room at a cafe and ordered a chocolate cake with her name written in blue icing. The difficult part is keeping the secret, because Nadia is very curious and asks too many questions. We have agreed to tell her that we are meeting for a study group. When she walks through the door, we will all shout surprise together. I am sure she will laugh, and maybe she will even cry a little.
tongue_twisters: Chocolate cake with creamy blue icing.
Secret surprises start with simple plans.
Nadia notices nearly everything.

title: Helping a Lost Tourist
paragraph: On my way to the bus stop yesterday, a tourist stopped me and asked for directions to the national museum. He held a crumpled map and looked a little confused. I explained that he should walk straight, turn left at the traffic light, and continue until he sees a large white building. He thanked me warmly and asked whether the museum was open on Fridays. I wasn't certain, so I suggested checking the website. As he walked away, I felt happy that I could help a stranger in a small but useful way.
tongue_twisters: Turn left at the tall traffic light.
The tourist took a thin, torn map.
Walk straight, then stop at the white building.

title: Fixing a Broken Bicycle
paragraph: Last weekend, the chain on my bicycle snapped halfway down the road. Instead of walking home, I pushed the bike to a small repair shop run by an old man named Karim. He examined the chain carefully, replaced a few links, and oiled the wheels until they spun smoothly. The whole repair took twenty minutes and cost almost nothing. While he worked, he told me stories about the bicycles he had fixed over forty years. I left the shop with a working bike and a new appreciation for people who repair things with patience.
tongue_twisters: The broken bicycle chain snapped suddenly.
Karim carefully checks each chain link.
Smooth wheels spin swiftly down the street.
